description: We are PinkSpectrum, a team of engineering students passionate about space and technology that helps people. We are building AstroCare, an offline-first app that helps astronauts monitor their health and make informed decisions when Earth is out of reach. Our skills include frontend and backend development, data, UI/UX design, and research.
summary:
AstroCare is an offline health copilot for astronauts on long deep-space missions. On a Mars mission a message to Earth can take up to 22 minutes each way, so the crew must notice and handle health changes on board. AstroCare runs entirely on one laptop with no internet connection.

It brings together vital signs, sleep, attention tests, exercise, cabin air, and radiation and bone-loss estimates, and compares each astronaut with their own baseline instead of population averages. When something changes, 12 transparent rules raise plain-language alerts that state what changed, which data was used, what is missing, the possible factors (never causes), and safe next steps checked against on-board medicines, equipment and allergies. Any step that involves a medicine is locked for the crew medical officer.

A local AI assistant answers questions from 18 saved NASA and CSA sources and the crew member's own data, and refuses medication and diagnosis questions. Reports for the flight surgeon wait in an outbox until the next communication window.

All demo data is simulated and labelled SIMULATED. AstroCare turns NASA's human-spaceflight hazards into something a crew can watch, understand and act on without waiting for Earth.
details:
THE PROBLEM

On a Mars mission the signal delay can reach up to 44 minutes round trip, and contact may be limited to scheduled communication windows. Crews must manage health concerns with limited equipment, medicines and medical support. A single health reading rarely explains the situation: its meaning depends on medical history, recent activity, data quality and cabin conditions. Our question was: how can health data become clear information and useful next steps that match the astronaut's condition and the mission's resources, even without a connection to Earth?

OUR SOLUTION

AstroCare is a working prototype of an offline-first health monitoring and decision-support application for the crew member and the crew medical officer (CMO). It runs entirely on one device, with a local rule engine and a local AI assistant, and every core function works with no connection to Earth. It tracks vital signs, sleep, attention, exercise, cabin conditions, an estimated radiation dose, an estimated bone-loss range and a vision self-check. It compares each astronaut with their own baseline and raises plain-language alerts that say what changed, what data is missing and what the possible factors are, with next steps checked against the crew's allergies and on-board supplies. A local assistant explains the data with sources and refuses medication and diagnosis questions. Reports for the flight surgeon wait in an outbox until the next communication window. AstroCare never diagnoses or prescribes.

HOW WE SOLVED EACH PART OF THE CHALLENGE

- Gather indicators: heart rate, SpO2, skin temperature, respiration and blood pressure, plus sleep, vision checks, reaction tests and mood and stress check-ins entered in the app.

- Enable self-assessment: the Today page, vitals trends against personal baselines, colour-coded body-system tiles, a 3D digital twin and explained alerts.

- Guide follow-up action: next steps link to retests, the daily log, exercise alternatives and available resources. Medicines and diagnosis stay with the CMO.

- Work within mission constraints: everything runs locally, and reports wait in an outbox for the next communication window.

HOW IT WORKS

- Everything runs on a single device: a React web interface, a local FastAPI server with a SQLite database (one file), a rule engine, and a local language model through Ollama.

- Every reading is stored with its source (sensor, manual, simulated or dataset), its quality and the sensor that produced it. The app shows each value with its age, quality and sensor status.

- The rule engine loads every rule file, runs it on a read-only context and stores new alerts. It does not create a second alert while the same one is still open. Every next step that names a medicine or equipment is checked for allergy conflict, expiry and stock, and medicine steps are always locked for the CMO.

- All thresholds live in one configuration file. Each has a source, or an honest "experimental / team decision" label where no published cut-off exists.

- While the server runs, a live feed adds heart rate, SpO2 and respiration every 5 minutes and cabin readings every 15 minutes, always inside normal ranges.

- A sensor adapter documents how a real wearable (for example the CSA Bio-Monitor shirt) or a dataset would fill the same tables. Rules read only through one context object, so changing the data source does not change the rules.

FEATURES (15 pages in four groups: Monitor, Daily, Space medicine, Support)

Every page shares a status bar (mission, local mode, next comm window, signal delay, outbox count, SIMULATED label, mission clock) and a red banner for crew emergencies.

- Today: mission day, new alerts, a sensor diagram, eight body-system tiles (cardiovascular, respiratory, sleep and circadian, cognition and behaviour, bone and muscle, radiation, vision and fluid shift, thermoregulation), vital cards against the personal baseline, cabin conditions with NASA limits, today's plan and a sleep summary. Blood pressure can be entered manually.

- Vitals: six tabs (heart rate, SpO2, skin temperature, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, respiration). The chart shades the personal baseline (mean ± 2 SD). Low-quality readings are drawn separately and left out of the average.

- Alerts and alert detail: every alert has the same five parts: what changed, data used, missing or unreliable data, possible factors, and next steps with resource status. Medicine steps show "CMO review required" and cannot be approved in the app. The crew can acknowledge an alert, copy a summary for a report, or use buttons such as "Retest now".

- Daily log: sleep chart with manual entry and a 1–5 rating; today's exercise from an example plan based on ISS devices (ARED, T2, CEVIS), with a "Couldn't do it" flow that offers ranked alternatives and drops any that need unavailable equipment; a mood and stress check-in with a private note.

- Attention check: a five-trial reaction test of about one minute. It shows the median, lapses and false starts against the person's own baseline; only a result 15 % or more slower is flagged. A retest opened from an alert shows before and after values and moves the alert to "recheck".

- Radiation: estimated cumulative dose against NASA's 600 mSv career limit, clearly labelled as an estimate.

- Bone and muscle: exercise adherence for the last seven days and an estimated bone-loss range; it states that bone density needs a DEXA scan on Earth.

- Vision check: a self-check for SANS (smallest readable line and an Amsler grid); a change offers "Add to report" and "Ask the assistant". It does not diagnose.

- Crew alerts: if at least two of four signals (sudden heart-rate change, chest signal lost, no wrist movement, low SpO2) start within 60 seconds, an urgent alert and a full-screen "Are you OK?" prompt appear. With no answer, the CMO and commander are alerted.

- Digital twin: a 3D body view whose regions show status from live data, with a timeline of mission days. It never reads private check-ins.

- Assistant: answers questions about the crew member's own data and the saved NASA and CSA references, with a mode badge, numbered sources, next steps and "Add to report".

- Resources: the crew kit of 10 equipment items and 15 medicines with quantity, expiry, status and contraindicated allergies, compared with the profile.

- Reports and Earth sync: the crew picks sections and items, then generates a PDF and JSON report. The outbox moves Draft, Ready, Queued, Sent; reports are sent only when the communication window opens.

- Relax: five scenes, nature sound, music or silence, 3, 5 or 10 minutes, and stress rated before and after. "Request support" adds a note to the next report.

- Profile: allergies, current medicines, medical history, personal baseline ranges and device status.

ALERT RULES (12)

R-DATA-01 stale or missing data; R-HR-01 heart rate above own baseline + 2 SD three times in a row; R-SPO2-01 SpO2 below 92 % for 5 minutes (a "recheck sensor" note if the readings are low quality); R-CAB-01 cabin CO2 above 3 mmHg (1-hour average); R-CAB-02 cabin temperature or humidity outside the comfort zone; R-CAB-03 cabin noise above its own recent history; R-SLP-01 short sleep on 2 of the last 3 nights; R-FAT-01 short sleep plus reaction time 15 % or more slower; R-CIRC-01 bedtimes shifting by more than 2 hours; R-EX-01 exercise missed 2 days in a row; R-VIS-01 vision check change; R-LOC-01 possible loss of consciousness.

DEMO STORY (mission day 142)

The crew member slept 4.9 and 5.1 hours on the last two nights, and their reaction median is 342 ms against a 285 ms baseline. The skin-temperature sensor has been disconnected for six hours, blood pressure is missing, and today's check-in is not done. AstroCare raises a "possible fatigue pattern" alert for review, lists the check-in as missing, and suggests a check-in, a retest after rest and a lighter workout. After a linked retest (295 ms, within the usual range) the alert moves to "recheck". The assistant explains the alert with NASA sources and refuses a melatonin question, and a report waits for the comm window.

SAFETY AND PRIVACY

- Medication and diagnosis questions are refused before they reach the model, with a button to send them to the CMO.

- Every medicine step is locked for the CMO; the app has no approval or administration function.

- Missing and low-quality data are never treated as normal measurements.

- Possible links between measurements are labelled "not a confirmed cause".

- Nothing leaves the device; sending to Earth is simulated.

- The assistant reads only an allow-list of fields. Check-ins are off by default, private notes never pass, and reports include check-ins only with permission.

- If the local model is off or too slow, a template built from the alert answers instead, so the assistant never goes silent.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, React Router, Recharts, lucide-react, local fonts, three.js and React Three Fiber.

Backend: Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, SQLite, NumPy, pandas, ReportLab, httpx.

Local AI: Ollama with Llama 3.2 3B and nomic-embed-text, retrieval over 18 saved reference files (51 passages).

Quality: pytest, TypeScript type-check, ESLint that blocks remote URLs, and an offline URL scanner.

Offline guarantee: no CDNs, remote fonts, images or APIs. Fonts and icons are bundled, the Relax images and audio were generated locally by the team, and a browser check with all non-local requests blocked recorded none.

TESTING AND CURRENT STATUS

The backend test suite and the TypeScript type check run with one command. A demo-state check runs 11 read-only checks of the starting state, and an assistant check confirms the local model and reference index are ready. A full simulated scenario was run end to end, from short sleep to a report marked sent in a simulated comm window. AstroCare is a working, offline-first prototype using simulated crew data. It has not been clinically validated, tested with real astronaut records, connected to flight sensors, or qualified for flight hardware.

LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK

Several thresholds are team decisions, not NASA medical trigger points, and need clinical review. Two are informed by published clinical guidance: SpO2 below 92 % matches the highest-risk SpO2 band of the NEWS2 early warning score (91 % or less), and short sleep under 6 h is well below the 7 h or more recommended for adults (AASM and Sleep Research Society) and close to the about 6 h astronauts average in flight (Barger et al., 2014). The 15 % attention change and the loss-of-consciousness conditions have no published cut-off.

USE OF AI TOOLS

In the app: a local Llama 3.2 3B model (Meta) and nomic-embed-text (Nomic AI), run through Ollama on the device, power the assistant only. No cloud AI service is used at runtime. During development: the team used an AI coding assistant (Claude by Anthropic) to help write, test and review code and draft documents. The team designed the product, made every decision, and reviewed and ran all code.
